readings.title: The lost teddy
readings.text: On the way home from the shops, Leo dropped his teddy bear. He did not notice until bedtime. He felt very sad and could not sleep. The next morning, Leo and his dad walked back along the street. There, sitting on a garden wall, was Teddy! A kind neighbour had put him there so that he would be easy to find.

readings.title: Busy ants
readings.text: Ants are tiny, but they are very strong. An ant can carry something much heavier than its own body. Ants live together in big groups called colonies. Each ant has a job. Some look after the eggs, some find food and some guard the nest. When an ant finds food, it leaves a smelly trail so the others can follow it.

questions.prompt: What is a group of ants called?
What can an ant carry?
Why does an ant leave a smelly trail?

readings.title: A day on the farm
readings.text: In the holidays, Aisha stayed on her uncle's farm. Every morning she got up early to help. First, she fed the hungry chickens. Then she watched her uncle milk the cows. In the afternoon, they drove the tractor to the field to pick strawberries. In the evening, Aisha was tired but happy. She could not wait to come back next summer.

readings.text: Zack built a robot from boxes, bottle tops and old wires. He called it Robo. Robo could not walk or talk, but Zack pretended that it could. readings.title: Night hunters
readings.text: Owls are birds that hunt at night. Their huge eyes help them to see in the dark, but they cannot move their eyes like we can. Instead, an owl can turn its head almost all the way round. Owls also have amazing hearing. Their soft feathers let them fly without making a sound, so mice and voles do not hear them coming. After a meal, an owl coughs up a pellet of bones and fur that it cannot digest.

questions.prompt: Why can owls turn their heads so far?
questions.explanation: «they cannot move their eyes ... Instead, an owl can turn its head»

questions.prompt: How do owls fly silently?
questions.explanation: «Their soft feathers let them fly without making a sound»

questions.prompt: What is an owl pellet?
options: Bones and fur it coughs up
questions.explanation: «a pellet of bones and fur that it cannot digest»

readings.title: The secret door
readings.text: In the corner of the school library there was a small wooden door that nobody ever opened. One rainy lunchtime, Priya noticed that it was slightly open. Inside, she found a tiny room full of old books, a dusty armchair and a lamp. On the table was a note: 'This reading room is for anyone who loves stories. Please look after it.' From that day on, Priya spent every rainy lunchtime there, lost in a new adventure.

questions.explanation: «In the corner of the school library»

questions.prompt: What did the note ask?

readings.title: Making a volcano
readings.text: For the science fair, Jamal decided to make a model volcano. He shaped a mountain from clay around an empty bottle and painted it brown and grey. Then he put some bicarbonate of soda inside the bottle. When he poured in vinegar with a drop of red food colouring, foam bubbled up and ran down the sides like lava. Everyone cheered. Jamal explained that the soda and vinegar react together and make a gas, which pushes the foam out.

readings.title: Saving water
readings.text: Clean water is precious. Although most of our planet is covered with water, only a tiny part of it is fresh water that we can drink. There are many easy ways to save it at home. You can turn off the tap while you brush your teeth, take a short shower instead of a bath, and fix dripping taps. A dripping tap can waste more than fifteen litres of water every day!

questions.prompt: What can we drink?
questions.explanation: «only a tiny part of it is fresh water that we can drink»

questions.prompt: What should you do while brushing your teeth?
questions.explanation: «turn off the tap while you brush your teeth»

questions.prompt: How much can a dripping tap waste in a day?
questions.explanation: «more than fifteen litres of water every day»

readings.title: The race
readings.text: Kofi had trained for months for the school cross-country race. On the day, it was cold and muddy. Halfway round, he was in second place when he saw a younger runner slip and fall in the mud. Kofi could have kept running, but he stopped and helped the boy to his feet. By the time they set off again, three runners had overtaken them. Kofi finished fifth. At the end of the day, the head teacher gave him a special award for sportsmanship, and Kofi realised that he was prouder of it than of any medal.

questions.prompt: What was the weather like?
Why did Kofi stop?
options: To help a runner who fell
questions.explanation: «he stopped and helped the boy to his feet»

questions.prompt: Why was Kofi proud?
options: He had done the right thing
questions.explanation: He got an award for sportsmanship.

readings.title: The printing press
readings.text: Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, usually by monks. It could take months to copy a single book, so books were rare and very expensive. Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg invented a printing press with metal letters that could be moved and reused. Suddenly, hundreds of copies could be printed quickly. Books became cheaper, more people learned to read, and ideas spread faster than ever before.

questions.prompt: Who copied books before the printing press?
What was special about Gutenberg's letters?
options: They could be moved and reused
questions.explanation: «metal letters that could be moved and reused»

questions.prompt: What was one result of the invention?

readings.title: The attic
readings.text: While helping Grandma clear out the attic, Rosa found a small tin box hidden behind a pile of old curtains. Inside were black-and-white photographs, a medal and a bundle of letters tied with ribbon. Grandma sat down slowly and smiled. 'These belonged to my father,' she said. 'He wrote these letters to my mother when he was a nurse during the war.' That afternoon, Rosa listened to stories she had never heard before, and the dusty attic suddenly felt like a treasure chest.

questions.prompt: Where was the tin box?

questions.prompt: Who did the letters belong to?

readings.title: Why we need bees
readings.text: About a third of the food we eat depends on pollination, and bees are some of the best pollinators. As a bee visits flowers to collect nectar, pollen sticks to its hairy body and is carried to the next flower. This helps plants to make fruit and seeds. Sadly, bee numbers are falling because of habitat loss, pesticides and disease. Planting wild flowers, avoiding chemical sprays and leaving some areas of grass to grow long are simple ways to help them.

questions.prompt: How much of our food depends on pollination?
questions.explanation: «About a third of the food we eat»

questions.prompt: How does pollen travel?
options: It sticks to the bee's body

questions.prompt: Which is a way to help bees?

readings.title: How the brain learns
readings.text: Every time you learn something new, tiny cells in your brain called neurons form new connections with each other. The more you practise, the stronger these connections become, rather like a path through a field that gets clearer each time someone walks along it. This is why practising a little every day is more effective than doing a lot once a week. Sleep also plays an important role: while you rest, your brain sorts and strengthens what you learned during the day. So making mistakes, practising and sleeping well are all part of learning.

questions.prompt: What are neurons?
questions.explanation: «tiny cells in your brain called neurons»

questions.prompt: Why is the brain compared to a path in a field?
questions.explanation: «a path ... that gets clearer each time someone walks along it»

questions.prompt: What happens while we sleep?
options: The brain strengthens what we learned
questions.explanation: «your brain sorts and strengthens what you learned»

readings.title: Stonehenge
readings.text: On Salisbury Plain in the south of England stands Stonehenge, a circle of enormous stones that was built in stages around five thousand years ago. Some of the stones weigh as much as twenty-five tonnes, and the smaller bluestones were brought from Wales, more than two hundred kilometres away. Nobody knows exactly why it was built, but on the longest day of the year the Sun rises in line with the stones, which suggests that the builders studied the sky carefully. Today, thousands of people visit it to watch the summer sunrise.

questions.prompt: When was Stonehenge built?
Where did the bluestones come from?
What suggests the builders studied the sky?
options: The Sun rises in line with the stones
questions.explanation: «the Sun rises in line with the stones»

readings.title: The last forest
readings.text: When the factory announced that it would cut down Hollow Wood, the town was divided. Some people hoped the new building would bring jobs; others could not imagine the town without its ancient trees. Fourteen-year-old Nia started a website where people could share their memories of the wood: first kisses, family picnics, the first time they saw a badger. Within weeks, thousands of stories had been posted. The factory's owners read them and decided to build on an empty car park instead. Hollow Wood is still there, and Nia's website has become a guide for other towns trying to protect their green spaces.

questions.prompt: Why were some people in favour of the factory?
What did Nia's website collect?
What made the owners change their minds?
questions.explanation: «read them and decided to build on an empty car park instead»

readings.title: Travelling words
readings.text: English is a language full of travellers. Many of its words arrived from other languages over hundreds of years. 'Pyjamas' and 'shampoo' came from India, 'chocolate' and 'tomato' from the Aztec language Nahuatl through Spanish, and 'kindergarten' from German. The Vikings gave us 'sky' and 'egg', while the Normans brought thousands of French words, such as 'beef' and 'castle'. Every time you speak English, you are using words that have crossed oceans and centuries to reach you.

questions.prompt: Where did 'pyjamas' come from?
Which words did the Vikings give English?
What is the main idea of the text?
options: English borrowed words from many languages
questions.explanation: The text explains the origins of English words.
